section: Late Submission and Incomplete Assignment Policy
text:
Late Submission and Incomplete Assignment Policy






Warning



Late submission is not allowed in this course.


I totally understand that as humans, things can sometimes come up or go wrong, and you are unable to get an assignment turned in on time. This kind of situation calls for some flexibility where I could consider accepting a late submission. However, this flexibility MUST be subject to my awareness and approval. Therefore, if any student is in this kind of unfortunate situation and would need more time to submit homework or the project a bit late, please contact me immediately.
I must receive an email and reply to it before the due date in order to implement this policy. As a matter of rule, no lateness beyond 1 day (24 hours) can be tolerated for any given homework/project. In some cases, a penalty (i.e., losing a portion or an entire grade for a particular submission) could be applied by the instructor based on the assessment of reasons for late submission, which is solely at the instructor’s discretion.
All students are allowed a maximum of two (2) late submissions in all assignments throughout the course, provided the late submission has been granted by the instructor following the protocol outlined above.

General Notes

Collaboration is highly expected in this course both during and outside of the classroom. Students will work together to understand how to solve the homework, complete projects, and other class activities.
Students are responsible for all missed work, regardless of the reason for absence. It is also the absentee’s responsibility to get all missing notes or materials.

title: Course Policies
section: Policy on the Use of AI and Generative AI
text:
Policy on the Use of AI and Generative AI
This is a course that heavily integrates Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Generative AI (GenAI) in designing interfaces for human use. As such, students are encouraged to explore and utilize these technologies responsibly. AI can be an excellent resource for:

Explaining complex concepts
Providing coding examples
Offering debugging suggestions
Recommending best practices
Exploring new ideas and approaches


Responsible Use and Academic Integrity
While the use of AI for learning is encouraged, it is crucial to maintain academic integrity and ensure genuine skill development. Therefore:

Do not use AI to directly solve all portions of assignments. Assignments are designed to develop your skills and understanding. Using AI to generate entire solutions when not instructed to do so is strictly prohibited.
Acknowledge AI usage. When you use AI or GenAI tools for inspiration or assistance in your workflow, you must clearly acknowledge this in your submissions. Include a brief note explaining how and where AI was used.
Understand what you submit. Ensure you review and understand any code or concepts you include in your work, regardless of whether AI assisted in generating them.



Warning: The Perils of Over-Reliance on AI
Over-reliance on AI for completing entire coursework may:

Hinder your learning — The hands-on experience of conceptualizing ideas, defining problems, and problem-solving is irreplaceable.
Impede your growth — Relying on AI prevents you from developing critical thinking skills essential for a career in UX/AI design.
Limit your creativity — Over-dependence can stifle your ability to come up with innovative solutions.
Compromise your future career — Employers value designers who can think independently and solve complex problems.







Warning



Consequences of Misuse: Misuse of AI tools, including using them to directly complete entire assignments without proper acknowledgment, will be treated as academic dishonesty and may result in disciplinary action.

title: Course Policies
section: Academic Honesty for Students in Computer Science
text:
Academic Honesty for Students in Computer Science
Academic integrity is crucial in your journey as a computer science student. The skills and knowledge you develop here will serve as the foundation for your future career.

Reasonable Actions

Talking with classmates about assignments — Engaging in discussions to clarify assignment requirements.
Discussing solution strategies verbally — Brainstorming and exchanging ideas, as long as no actual code is shared.
Whiteboarding a solution — Collaboratively working on diagrams, outlines, or pseudocode without writing actual code.
Referring classmates to helpful resources — Suggesting chapters, websites, or other materials.
Searching the web for general help — Looking for concepts that might aid in solving the problem, without seeking exact solutions.
Using a small amount of code from reliable sources — Incorporating minor code snippets from online or books, provided they are not the core of the solution and are properly cited.
Working with a tutor — Receiving help while ensuring all code written is your own.
Pairs programming during official activities — Collaboratively writing code with a partner as part of a designated pairs programming assignment.



Reasonable But Be Careful

Showing your code to another student — Sharing code for debugging purposes only, in a controlled, private setting.
Reviewing others’ code post-submission — Analyzing peers’ code after submission to enhance learning.



Not Reasonable

Submitting another student’s work as your own.
Copying from another student’s quiz or exam.
Viewing or copying another student’s solution.
Copying solutions from previous years.
Recording or sharing exam content.
Maintaining public repositories of course solutions.

Always remember: academic honesty is about ensuring that the work you submit is truly your own. If you are ever unsure about what is allowed, please ask the instructor for clarification.

title: AI 380: Human-AI Interaction
text:
Course Overview
This course introduces the core principles of human-centered design for conversational AI systems — including chatbots, virtual assistants, and interactive voice interfaces. Students explore how natural language processing (NLP), dialogue management, and user experience (UX) principles converge to create intuitive, accessible, and inclusive AI interactions.
Through hands-on projects, students learn to design, prototype, and rigorously evaluate conversational interfaces that handle real-world user intent while accounting for system limitations, user trust, and safety. We draw inspiration and methodology from leading programs at top HCI institutions.






Note



Prerequisite: CS 151 is required before taking this course. Students who have completed a software engineering course will find it an additional advantage — however, because of the interdisciplinary nature of this course, non-CS majors are strongly encouraged to enroll as well.
Course Note: This course requires group project work. Students who enroll must be ready to collaborate with peers on a substantial design and evaluation project throughout the semester.

Course Learning Objectives
By the end of this course, you will be able to:



01


Critique & Synthesize Research


Review scientific literature in human-AI interaction to synthesize trends, evaluate technological tradeoffs, and inform evidence-based design decisions.




02


Design Conversational Systems


Apply human-centered design principles alongside NLP and dialogue management frameworks to prototype and build functional, context-aware conversational interfaces.




03


Evaluate Usability & Ethics


Conduct rigorous usability testing to assess user trust, efficiency, and error recovery, while analyzing ethical risks, accessibility constraints, and AI failure modes.




04


Collaborate & Communicate


Work in multidisciplinary teams to manage interactive AI projects, communicating outcomes through professional presentations and technical reports.

title: Group Project
text:
Project 1: Conversation AI Learning Environment

Overview
In this first project, teams co-design and build an interactive VR learning experience for older adults (ages 70+) using the course’s custom web-authoring tool. The goal is to support cognitive health, memory, or daily routine management through a carefully designed 9-screen VR activity validated on the Meta Quest 3.
This project develops skills in: needfinding, paper prototyping, digital authoring, VR interaction design, and older adult UX considerations.


Milestones

Design Considerations for Older Adults
All VR activities must incorporate UX accommodations for users 70+:

Large UI targets — buttons and hotspots with generous touch/pointer areas
High-contrast visual cues — colors and borders that remain legible with reduced vision
Gentle pacing — no time pressure; patient transitions between screens
Audio support — important instructions read aloud, not text-only
Low-stress error recovery — positive feedback regardless of initial response; no penalties
Minimal cognitive load — linear layouts, one action per screen



Authoring Platform
Teams use the course web-authoring tool to build and export VR lessons:
http://147.182.173.208:5173/
The platform allows teams to author 9-screen interactive sequences and export them for deployment on the Meta Quest 3. Instructor will provide onboarding in Week 9 lab sessions.


Example Activity Scenarios



💊


Medication Management


Help older adults learn to organize, sort, and manage daily medications — sorting pills by meal timing, understanding label instructions, setting reminder alarms.




🧠


Memory Exercises


Sequence-based activities for short-term memory practice — ordering morning routine steps, matching terms, or completing daily checklists.




🏠


Daily Living Skills


Practice navigating everyday tasks — preparing an emergency kit, planning a grocery list, or reviewing home safety procedures.

Design Process Requirements
Each milestone builds on the previous, following the double-diamond design process:
Discover → Define → Develop → Deliver

Research Phase (Weeks 1–8)

Design Phase (Weeks 4–8)

Paper prototype conversational flows before building
Use Workshop 1 (Week 4) and Workshop 2 (Week 8) for structured ideation
Produce paper dialogue flowcharts for all major conversational paths



Build Phase (Weeks 9–11)

Use Rasa CALM as the conversational AI framework
Build in accessibility from the start (don’t retrofit)
Participate in Lab 2, Lab 3, and Lab 4 sessions for hands-on implementation support
Complete Docker containerization before GP3 deadline



Evaluation Phase (Weeks 12–14)

Conduct heuristic evaluation in Week 12 workshop with a peer team
Run user studies with at least 3 older adult participants (Nov–Dec)
Use think-aloud protocol + post-session questionnaire
CITI research ethics context applies — treat participants with care and respect

title: Group Project
text:
Project FAQ
Do we choose our own project topic within Project 2?
Yes. Teams choose the specific domain (cognitive, mobility, or social) and the exact problem to solve. The constraint is that the target population is older adults (70+) and the system must be a conversational AI interface.
Can we build a real system, not just a prototype?
Yes — and you are encouraged to. Using Rasa CALM to build a functional conversational agent is required for GP3. Technical sophistication is valued, but the primary focus for grading is the design process and evaluation rigor, not how many features you ship.
What if we cannot recruit older adult participants?
Contact the instructor immediately. The class Discord has a #participant-recruitment channel. The instructor can provide access to community partner networks. Do not simply substitute CS students for your target population.
How should we handle a teammate who is not contributing?
First, address it within your team using the Work Agreement. If unresolved, contact the instructor with documentation. Individual grades may be adjusted based on contribution evidence.
What technology is required for GP3?
Rasa CALM (or equivalent enterprise conversational AI framework), Docker for containerization, and a web or mobile frontend. Specific framework choices should be discussed with the instructor by GP2.
Can we use ChatGPT or other LLMs in our system?
Yes. AI-augmented prototypes are encouraged. Document your use of AI tools in your report, including what they were used for and any limitations observed.

Individual Homework Assignments

HW0 — Personal Introduction & Expectations
Due: Thursday, Aug 28 · Canvas Discussion Board · Participation


Objective
Introduce yourself to your peers and articulate your goals, prior background, and expectations for this course.


Instructions
Post a brief response on the Canvas Discussion Board covering:

Basic Introduction — Name, major/academic year, and a brief note on your prior experience with Computer Science, Data/AI, or Design.
Course Expectations — What specific topic or skill in Human-AI Interaction are you most excited to learn (e.g., conversational design, user research, rapid prototyping, ethical AI)?
Real-World AI Systems — Name one interactive AI system or tool you use regularly (e.g., ChatGPT, code completion tools, recommendation systems). What is one thing it does exceptionally well from a user perspective, and one failure mode or design flaw you have noticed?



Submission
Post directly to the Canvas Discussion Board by Aug 28. Reply to at least one classmate’s post.





HW1 — Critical Literature Synthesis & Interface Critique
Due: Friday, Sep 5 (11:59 PM) · 3%


Description
Write a 300-word position paper analyzing an AI tool through the lens of the Week 1–2 readings.


Tasks

Select an intelligent everyday application (e.g., ChatGPT, email smart reply, or a recommendation engine).
Critique the application using the tension between Direct Manipulation vs. Interface Agents (Shneiderman & Maes, 1997) and Power to the People (Amershi et al., 2014).
Evaluate how effectively the tool supports human agency versus over-automating decisions.
Propose two concrete UX redesigns to resolve the identified issues.



Submission
Submit a PDF to Canvas. Include screenshots to support your critique.

10

20

HW2 — Applied Needfinding & Low-Fidelity Prototype
Due: Thursday, Sep 18 (11:59 PM) · 3%


Description
Produce a 2–3 page project discovery report and an initial paper prototype for an individual design concept.


Tasks

Observation & Persona — Conduct a brief participant observation session (15–20 min) of a user interacting with an existing intelligent application. Construct 1–2 user personas based on observed pain points, referencing Klemmer’s observation video (Week 3) and Visme’s persona-creation method.
Problem Critique — Identify user-reported issues (loss of control, unpredictability, or lack of transparency) inspired by When People and Algorithms Meet (Eslami et al., IUI 2019).

title: Assignments
text:
Final Reflection Essay
Due: Saturday, Dec 5 · 10%


Description
Write an individual reflection essay (800–1,200 words). This is a reflective synthesis — not a summary of the course.
Address all four prompts:

Most important insight — What is the most important thing you learned about designing AI systems for human use? Give a concrete example from your project or the course.
Changed thinking — How did your perspective on AI and society shift over the semester? What challenged your assumptions?
Ethical dimension — Choose one ethical issue in AI design (fairness, transparency, privacy, manipulation, access) and describe how you would address it as a designer.
Looking forward — What aspect of Human-AI Interaction do you most want to explore further? What question do you wish this course had answered?



Submission
Submit individually via Canvas. Do not share with teammates before submitting.

Criterion
Points




Depth and specificity of reflection
30


Connection to course concepts and readings
25


Evidence of changed or nuanced thinking
20


Writing quality (clarity, voice, flow)
15


Forward-looking insight
10

100 points









Tip



Strong essays make specific references to readings, in-class activities, or project experiences — not just generic statements about AI. Show your thinking process, not just your conclusions.

text:
How to Read Academic Papers
Reading HCI research papers is a skill. For each required paper, aim to:

Skim first — abstract, intro, conclusions, figures (5 min)
Identify the main claim — what do the authors argue, and what evidence supports it?
Note what surprised you — bring one observation to class
Assess transferability — how does this apply to your project or a system you know?

For long readings, focus on the sections indicated in the schedule. Full papers are provided for context.

section: Module 1: Human-AI Interaction and User-Centered Design
text:
Module 1: Human-AI Interaction and User-Centered Design
Foundations of HCI, the role of humans in AI, design thinking, needfinding, and user research. Establishes the vocabulary and frameworks underpinning all human-centered design practice — and situates conversational AI within the broader HCI tradition.


Week 1 — Aug 24 & 26 · Introduction to Human-AI Interaction




Monday, Aug 24 First Day


Kick-off: Introduction, Logistics & Design Overview


Lecture



Welcome to AI 380. We introduce the field of Human-AI Interaction, survey the landscape of conversational AI systems — chatbots, voice assistants, recommendation engines — and establish why design matters for AI. Course logistics, expectations, and team formation overview.



Wednesday, Aug 26


The Role of Humans in AI


Lecture



What is the relationship between humans and machine learning systems? We examine interactive ML, human-in-the-loop design, and the fundamental tension between automation and human control.


Readings Due Aug 28:

Power to the People: The Role of Humans in Interactive Machine Learning. AI Magazine.



Due Aug 28: HW0 — Personal Introduction & Expectations (Canvas Discussion Board)




Week 2 — Aug 31 & Sep 2 · Historical Perspectives & Everyday AI




Monday, Aug 31


A Historical Perspective of Human-AI Interaction


Lecture



From early command-line interfaces to today’s large language models — how did we get here? We trace the arc of human-computer interaction, highlighting where AI shifted the design paradigm from direct manipulation to delegated agency.



Wednesday, Sep 2 No Show Roster


Everyday AI Applications


Lecture



AI is embedded in the tools we use every day — and often fails us in everyday ways. We examine user-reported problems with intelligent applications and discuss the gulf between what AI promises and what it delivers.


Readings Due Sep 5:

Dijkstra, E.W. (1978). On the Foolishness of “Natural Language Programming.”.
Shneiderman, B. & Maes, P. (1997). Direct Manipulation vs. Interface Agents. Interactions.
When People and Algorithms Meet: User-Reported Problems in Intelligent Everyday Applications. IUI 2019.



Due Sep 4 (Last Day Add/Drop)
Due Sep 5: HW1 — Critical Literature Synthesis & Interface Critique




Week 3 — Sep 7 & 9 · Design Process & Persuasive Design




Monday, Sep 7


Labor Day — No Class


Holiday




Wednesday, Sep 9


Design Process & Persuasive Design


Lecture



IDEO’s design thinking process: Empathize → Define → Ideate → Prototype → Test. We apply the framework to AI system design and examine BJ Fogg’s Persuasive Technology model — how AI systems nudge, influence, and sometimes manipulate user behavior.


Readings Due Sep 14:

IDEO. Design Thinking. Online resource.
Brainstorm, Chainstorm, Cheatstorm, Tweetstorm: Ideation Methods.
Fogg, B.J. The Process of Persuasion. Interaction Design Foundation.





Week 4 — Sep 14 & 16 · Understanding Users & Personas




Monday, Sep 14


Understanding Users & Personas


Lecture



How do we learn what users actually need? We cover participant observation, contextual inquiry, and interview techniques. We then translate user research into personas — actionable archetypes that guide design decisions throughout the project lifecycle.



Wednesday, Sep 16


Users Domain and Context: Understanding Older Adults and Ageism (with Tommy Van Cleave)


Guest Session



Guest session with Tommy Van Cleave exploring users’ domain and context — with a specific focus on understanding older adults and ageism. How do we design conversational AI systems that truly serve the needs and cognitive patterns of elderly users?

Klemmer, S. (2013). Participant Observation. 6-min video. HCI MOOC, Stanford.

title: Course Schedule
text:
Module 2: Human-AI Collaborations
Conversational AI design, human-AI collaboration challenges, dialogue management guidelines, and lab work building Rasa-powered conversational agents.


Week 5 — Sep 21 & 23 · Conversational AI & Lab 1




Monday, Sep 21


Human-AI Interaction: A Conversational Agent


Lecture



Introducing the conversational agent as an interaction paradigm. What distinguishes a conversational interface from a GUI? We examine the design space — text-based chatbots, voice assistants, multimodal agents — and discuss the expectations users bring to each type.



Wednesday, Sep 23


Lab 1: Human-in-the-Loop Systems and Human-AI Collaboration


Lab



Hands-on lab. Students explore human-in-the-loop design by building a simple conversational prototype and experimenting with different levels of automation and user control. Introduces the Rasa development environment.


Readings Due Sep 28:

Luger, E. & Sellen, A. (2016). “Like Having a Really Bad PA”: The Gulf between User Expectation and Experience of Conversational Agents. CHI 2016.
Interaction Design Foundation. What Is User Interface Design?



Due Sep 25: GP0 — Team Formation, Charter & Project Journal Setup




Week 6 — Sep 28 & Sep 30 · Challenges, Guidelines & Workshop 1




Monday, Sep 28


Challenges and Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction


Lecture



Why is designing for AI-mediated interactions uniquely difficult? We examine fundamental challenges — opacity of AI decision-making, miscalibrated user trust, brittleness, and explainability — then walk through Microsoft’s 18 guidelines for Human-AI Interaction and discuss which apply to conversational AI.



Wednesday, Sep 30


Workshop 1 with Older Adults: Empathize, Define, and Ideate


Workshop



Hands-on workshop with older adult participants. Teams practice the first three stages of design thinking — empathy mapping, POV synthesis, and structured ideation — informed by the challenges and guidelines of human-AI interaction. Real user participation provides direct design insights.


Readings Due Oct 5:

Cai, C.J., et al. (2019). Re-examining Whether, Why, and How Human-AI Interaction Is Uniquely Difficult to Design. CHI 2020.
Amershi, S., et al. (2019). Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. CHI 2019.



Due Oct 2: GP1 — Co-Designing & Authoring VR Interventions for Older Adults




Week 7 — Oct 5 & 7 · Conversational AI (1) & Midterm Quiz




Monday, Oct 5


Conversational AI and AI Assistants (Part 1): Introduction


Lecture



Introduction to the conversational AI ecosystem: rule-based systems, retrieval-based chatbots, generative LLMs, and task-oriented dialogue systems. We examine the CALM (Conversational AI with Language Models) paradigm and how Rasa Pro implements it.



Wednesday, Oct 7


Midterm Quiz


Quiz



In-class midterm quiz covering Modules 1–2 content: HCI fundamentals, design thinking, needfinding methods, conversational AI design principles, and Human-AI Interaction guidelines.


Readings Due Oct 12:

Human-AI Interaction & GenAI. CHI 2026 Podcast — link on Canvas.
Freed, A.R. (2021). Conversational AI. Chapter 1. PDF on Canvas.



Key Date Oct 9: Mid-semester break — No class




Week 8 — Oct 12 & 14 · Conversational AI (2) & (3)




Monday, Oct 12


Conversational AI and AI Assistants (Part 2): Designing for Success


Lecture



What separates good conversational AI design from bad? We examine dialogue management patterns — happy paths, fallbacks, clarification loops, and graceful degradation. Case studies from commercial assistants (Alexa, Google Assistant) and enterprise chatbots.



Wednesday, Oct 14


Conversational AI and AI Assistants (Part 3): Training and Testing


Lecture



How do you train and test conversational AI systems? We cover data collection, intent annotation, training pipelines, and testing strategies — including automated testing, unit tests for dialogue flows, and end-to-end conversation simulation. Accessibility and ethical responsibilities for AI designers per WCAG.


Readings Due Oct 19:

Weiser, M. (1991). The Technologist’s Responsibilities and Social Change..
W3C. Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1.



Due Oct 16: GP2 — User Needfinding, Personas & Paper Conversational Workflow

title: Course Schedule
section: Module 3: AI Design and Conversational Orchestration
text:
Module 3: AI Design and Conversational Orchestration
Deep-dive into building AI assistants with Rasa CALM — from architecture through training, testing, and deployment. Three hands-on lab sessions guide teams through implementation of their conversational AI assistant.


Week 9 — Oct 19 & 21 · CALM Architecture & Lab 2




Monday, Oct 19


Conversational AI with Language Model (CALM)


Lecture



Deep dive into Rasa Pro’s CALM (Conversational AI with Language Models) architecture: flows, commands, actions, domain, and slot management. How CALM differs from traditional intent-based NLU and why it produces more robust multi-turn dialogue.



Wednesday, Oct 21


Lab 2: CALM with Rasa Framework


Lab



Hands-on lab: teams set up the Rasa development environment, implement their first CALM flow, define custom actions, and test basic multi-turn dialogue. Students begin mapping their GP2 conversational workflows into Rasa YAML configs.


Readings Due Oct 26:

Rasa. Rasa Documentation — CALM Overview.



Key Date Oct 23: Last day to withdraw from full-semester class




Week 10 — Oct 26 & 28 · CALM Overview & Lab 3




Monday, Oct 26


CALM Overview: NLU, Flows, and Dialogue Management


Lecture



Comprehensive review of CALM components: intent classification, entity extraction, flow conditions, slot filling, and action server integration. Discussion of common failure modes and how to debug Rasa dialogue predictions using the Rasa Inspector.



Wednesday, Oct 28


Lab 3: CALM with Rasa Framework


Lab



Lab continuation: teams implement custom actions (API calls, database lookups), add entity-based slot filling, and test fallback handling. Instructor and TAs provide hands-on debugging support.


Readings Due Nov 2:

Rasa. Rasa Documentation — Actions & Custom Actions.
Rasa. Rasa Documentation — Actions & Custom Actions.





Week 11 — Nov 2 & 4 · Building for Success & Lab 4




Monday, Nov 2


AI Assistant: Building for Success


Lecture



What makes an AI assistant succeed with real users? We examine best practices for intent coverage, response quality, graceful error handling, and inclusive design. Case studies from deployed elder-care and accessibility-focused AI systems.



Wednesday, Nov 4


Lab 4: CALM with Rasa Framework


Lab



Final Rasa lab: teams complete their full dialogue system, integrate the web/voice interface, and conduct internal QA testing. Focus on accessibility features (large UI targets, speech-to-text integration, high-contrast styling) and containerizing with Docker for GP3.


Readings Due Nov 9:

Rasa. Rasa Documentation — Deployment & Channels.



Key Date Nov 3: Only lab-format classes meet (check Canvas for schedule)

title: Course Schedule
section: Module 4: User Experience, Usability Study, Report & Presentation
text:
Module 4: User Experience, Usability Study, Report & Presentation
Usability testing, heuristic evaluation, ethical AI design, peer review, and final project presentations. Students evaluate their systems with real older adult users and communicate findings professionally.


Week 12 — Nov 9 & 11 · Usability Testing & Heuristic Evaluation




Monday, Nov 9


AI Assistant: Training and Testing


Lecture



How do you evaluate a conversational AI system? We cover intent accuracy metrics, conversation quality metrics, task completion rates, and user satisfaction scales. Discussion of mixed-methods evaluation: combining quantitative logs with qualitative think-aloud data.



Wednesday, Nov 11


Usability Study and Heuristic Evaluation


Workshop



In-class workshop: peer heuristic evaluation of each team’s conversational AI system. Teams apply Nielsen’s 10 heuristics to a classmate’s prototype and produce severity-rated findings. Discussion of how to run user studies with older adult participants.


Readings Due Nov 13:

Freed, A.R. (2021). Conversational AI. Chapter 11. PDF on Canvas.
Nielsen, J. (1994). How to Conduct a Heuristic Evaluation. Nielsen Norman Group.
Klemmer, S. Heuristic Evaluation Lecture..



Due Nov 13: HW3 — Heuristic Evaluation Report




Week 13 — Nov 16 & 18 · Interface Testing & Documentation




Monday, Nov 16


Workshop 2: Interface Testing with Users & Usability Study (Field Experiment with Older Adults)


Workshop



In-class share-out: teams present preliminary findings from field user tests with older adults (task completion rates, usability friction, key observations, think-aloud excerpts). Instructor and peers provide feedback on findings interpretation and GP4 report direction.



Wednesday, Nov 18


Project Documentation and Communication Strategy


Lecture



What makes a great HCI project report? Academic writing conventions, figure/table design, and telling a coherent design story. How to give an effective technical presentation with a live demo. Teams outline their GP4 reports.


Readings Due Nov 23:

Ethics Pathways in HCI Research..



Due Nov 20: GP3 — System Implementation, Integration & Containerization
Key Date Nov 17: Spring 2027 registration begins




Week 14 — Nov 23 & 25 · Peer Review & Fall Break




Monday, Nov 23


Future Technologies & Project Peer Review


Workshop



Structured peer-review session: teams share an executive summary and prototype demo. Reviewers provide structured written feedback using the GP4 rubric. Discussion of emerging AI interfaces — wearables, ambient intelligence, and embodied AI — and what “Human-AI Interaction” will mean when the interface disappears.



Wednesday, Nov 25


Fall Break — No Class


Break



Readings Due Nov 30:

Eagleman, D. (2015). Can We Create New Senses for Humans? TED Talk (video).



Key Date Nov 25–27: Fall Break — University closed




Week 15 — Nov 30 & Dec 2 · Project Exhibition & Final Reflection




Monday, Nov 30


🎤 Project Presentation Check-in


Check-in



Pre-exhibition check-in session. Teams share their final system status, present key findings, and receive instructor and peer feedback before the Wednesday exhibition. Opportunity to refine presentation and demo.



Wednesday, Dec 2


🎓 Project Presentation Exhibition & Finals Review/Reflection


Exhibition



Final public project exhibition. All teams demonstrate their completed conversational AI systems and present their design process and evaluation findings. Followed by course-wide Finals Review and Reflection. Key date: Dec 4 is the last day of class.


Due Dec 2: Final Presentation and Course Reflection Essay
Due Dec 3: GP4 — Public Deployment, Usability Testing & Final Documentation
Key Date Dec 4: Last day of class

text:
1. Lectures
Lectures and class activities will be held every Monday and Wednesday from August 24 through December 4, 2026, except for university holidays. Slides and resources are accessible from the Canvas course page. Full class attendance and participation are mandatory and are graded.

title: AI 380: Course Syllabus
text:
2. Weekly Readings and Homework
Weekly readings are to be completed individually before class to prepare for discussions. Class activities may include:

Short quizzes or reading responses
Open dialogue and Socratic discussion
Collaborative in-class design exercises
“Teaser” activities to connect readings to real AI systems

There will also be 3–4 individual homework assignments and one individual short project throughout the semester.

This course centers on two major group project requiring 2–3 members per group. title: AI 380: Course Syllabus
text:
Academic Honesty
Cheating is defined as any form of intellectual dishonesty or misrepresentation of one’s knowledge. Plagiarism — intentionally or unintentionally representing someone else’s work as your own — is strictly prohibited.
Penalties may range from a grade reduction on an assignment to failing the course. An instructor can also involve the Office of the Dean of the School of Computing and Information Sciences for further action. For further information, read the School of Computing and Information Science students handbook and also see the Willamette Academic Integrity Policy for full details.
Regarding AI Tools: Students are expected to disclose any use of AI writing or coding assistants. For design projects, AI-assisted prototyping tools are permitted and encouraged as part of learning the ecosystem. AI-generated text submitted as original writing without disclosure is a violation of academic integrity.
